subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 16 periods = 640 minutes
Total: 16 periods · 10h 40min

periods.activity_title: Our Address on Earth — Globe Hunt
periods.textbook_anchor: The Blue Planet — Students fill in their full personal address from name to planet and use a globe to find whether all oceans are connected (p. 162)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens by asking: 'If you were looking down at Earth from very high up in space, what do you think you would see — lines between countries, or something else?' Students share briefly. Teacher reads aloud the reflection by Shubhanshu Shukla from Textbook p. 162, pausing to let students respond to the idea that no borders are visible from space.

Students open Textbook p. 162 and individually complete the address activity — filling in every level from their own name down to 'Planet Earth'. Teacher circulates, inviting students to notice how the address moves from the smallest scale (their name) to the largest (planet). After writing, two or three students read their addresses aloud; the class notices the shared final line.

Working in pairs, students use the globe to explore whether all the oceans on Earth are connected, then locate India (Textbook p. 162). Pairs discuss: 'If the oceans are all joined, what does that mean for animals or ships moving across them?' Teacher notes the DIGIPIN fact from the textbook as a brief aside — that every location on Earth now has a digital address — connecting it to the idea of a shared, mappable planet.

Whole-class discussion: 'The textbook says nature has no boundaries — air, water, clouds, seeds, and animals move freely. Can you think of one example you have seen or heard of?' Students share one example each. Teacher closes by posing the question that will run through the chapter: 'If nature shares itself so freely, what does that mean for how we should treat the Earth and each other?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can locate geographic features on a globe and articulate why natural features do not align with human-made boundaries.
periods.section_context: Personal address from name to planet, globe exploration of connected oceans, locating India on a globe, DIGIPIN digital address system, Shubhanshu Shukla's borderless Earth reflection, Rakesh Sharma's 'Saare Jahaan Se Achcha'.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether anyone has a family member who has moved to a different city or country — this opens the idea of shared but unbounded spaces naturally. Keep the globe-work unhurried so every pair actually traces the ocean connection rather than just guessing.

periods.activity_title: Rosy Starlings on the Globe — Tracing Migration
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 1: The Travelling Birds! — Students use a string on a globe to trace the migration path of rosy starlings from Russia and Mongolia to India (p. 165)
materials: Coloured string or wool (one piece per pair)
Tape or sticky putty to anchor string
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image of rosy starlings; globe

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the rosy starling story from Textbook p. 165, pausing after the description of how these birds feed on locusts to ask: 'Why would farmers welcome these visitors from so far away?' Students notice the mutual benefit — the birds get warmth, the farmers get pest control — establishing that migration is not random but purposeful.

In pairs, students use a piece of coloured string and the globe to trace the rosy starling migration route: from Russia and Mongolia to India, as described in Textbook p. 165. Each pair marks the rough start point, runs the string across the globe, and marks the arrival region in India. They record in their notebooks: the countries the birds cross, the approximate direction of travel, and one observation about the distance.

Pairs share their route observations with the class. Teacher draws out: 'The birds cross national borders freely — Russia, Central Asia, India. Does the bird ask permission? What does this tell us about how nature works?' Students respond to both questions in their notebooks as a short written reflection.

Students answer in their notebooks (from Textbook p. 164): 'What does this story tell us about nature?' — in two or three sentences. Teacher invites one or two responses. Class closes with the question: 'Do you think birds in your area might have come from somewhere else? What would you look for to find out?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can use a globe to trace a migration route and record directional observations about movement across geographic boundaries.
periods.section_context: Rosy starlings, migration route from Russia and Mongolia to India, locusts and grasshoppers as food source, farmers benefiting from bird arrivals, string-tracing on globe.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students to consider whether their own families have ever migrated — even within India — to draw out that migration is a shared experience of people and animals alike. If students ask about local bird names for the rosy starling, encourage them to ask elders at home and bring the answer next time they meet.

periods.activity_title: Winter Birds Inquiry — Making a Poster
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 1: The Travelling Birds! — Students make a poster of five birds that visit their place in winter and find out where they come from (p. 165)
materials: Reference cards or simple bird guides provided by teacher (optional)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of rosy starlings (p. 165) as a reference model

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a short inquiry question: 'How would a scientist find out which birds visit a place in winter?' Students brainstorm methods — looking, asking people, checking books, noticing what they eat. This frames the poster task not as art but as an inquiry record.

Students work individually on the poster task from Textbook p. 165 — drawing and labelling five birds that visit their place in winter, with a note for each on where it might come from. Students who are unsure of five birds begin with what they know and fill gaps through a short whole-class sharing of bird names. Teacher circulates, asking guiding questions: 'Do you know what this bird eats? Does it stay year-round or only in winter?'

Four or five students hold up their posters and name one bird with its likely origin. Class compares: are some birds the same across posters? Do some students know a different local name for the same bird? Teacher notes that different communities often have different names for the same bird — an example of how local knowledge and scientific knowledge exist together.
Students write one sentence in their notebooks: 'One thing I want to find out about birds in my area is…' This keeps inquiry open without promising a specific follow-up activity.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple guided inquiry to identify local examples of a natural phenomenon and record their findings in a visual format.
periods.section_context: Winter birds visiting a local area, rosy starling as model migratory bird, local names for birds, birds' origins in other countries.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Invite students to share any bird names they have heard from grandparents or farmers in their family — folk names for migratory birds are often richly descriptive and link local knowledge to the scientific story. Keep the drawing phase purposeful — label and origin matter more than artistic finish.

periods.activity_title: Bird's-Eye Postcard — Writing from a Traveller's View
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 1: The Travelling Birds! — Students imagine they are a bird travelling the world and write a short postcard about what they see and what helps them on their journey (p. 165)
materials: A5-sized blank paper cut to postcard shape (one per student)
Coloured pencils for simple illustration on reverse (optional)

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets the scene: 'You are a rosy starling. You have just left Mongolia in autumn. You are flying south. What do you see below you? What pushes you along?' Class brainstorms aloud — mountains, rivers, different landscapes, wind currents, warmth — drawing from the story content and the globe work done with the migration route.

Students write their postcard from Textbook p. 165 — short, first-person, addressed to 'a friend back in Mongolia'. The postcard should mention at least one thing seen during the journey and one thing that helped the bird travel (wind, warm weather, ocean currents). Teacher circulates, prompting shy writers with: 'What is the most surprising thing your bird notices about India?' Students may add a small drawing on the reverse.

Students share their postcards in groups of four by reading them aloud. Group members give one word of feedback — 'vivid', 'surprising', 'funny' — and identify whether each postcard mentioned something from nature that helped the journey. Teacher draws out the connection: even a creative piece like a postcard carries real observations about how migration works.

Whole-class close: 'What does it mean when we say nature has no boundaries?' (Textbook p. 165). Students offer brief verbal answers. Teacher accepts all responses and frames the idea that the bird's freedom to travel is the same freedom seeds, water, and ideas have — linking forward to the chapter's broader theme without naming any unit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present observations about a natural process through a creative written mode, including factual details within an imaginative format.
periods.section_context: Rosy starling migration, wind and ocean currents as travel aids, warm weather in India, Mongolia and Russia as origin points, nature's lack of boundaries.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage students to use their own language if they find English difficult — the content matters more than the language register at this stage. Ask: 'Did anyone's bird notice something that surprised them? Something from a different country that felt familiar?' This draws out the idea of shared natural features across borders.

periods.activity_title: Yoga Across the World — Discussion and Pose Exploration
periods.section_ref: Story 2: Yoga—India's Gift to the World!
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 2: Yoga—India's Gift to the World! — Students discuss why yoga became popular in so many countries and name a yoga pose they have tried or seen (p. 167)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens: 'Has anyone here ever done yoga, or seen someone doing it — at home, in school, or on a screen?' Students share briefly. Teacher then reads the key facts from the textbook: yoga is about 3,000 years old, it started in India, and on 21 June every year, people all over the world practise it together. Students are asked: 'How does something that started in one country end up being practised everywhere?'

Whole-class discussion on Textbook p. 167: 'Why do you think yoga became popular in so many countries?' Teacher records student ideas on the board under two headings: 'What yoga does for the body' and 'How it spread'. Students draw on the textbook's explanation (travellers, scholars, teachers spreading it) and their own knowledge. Teacher draws out the idea that yoga's roots in harmony with nature and one's own body gave it appeal beyond any single culture.

Students write in their notebooks (Textbook p. 167): 'Name a yoga pose you have tried or seen. What do you think it helps with?' Students who know a pose name it and describe its effect; those who do not may describe what they see when someone does yoga — stillness, balance, stretching — and hypothesise what it does. Teacher accepts all responses; the point is to connect personal experience to the cultural practice.

Class discussion: 'If yoga is 3,000 years old and it came from India, is it still Indian? Or does it belong to everyone now?' Students offer views. Teacher connects this to the chapter's theme: some things travel so far and become so widely loved that they become shared human heritage — the idea of Earth as a shared home, not just for birds and plants but for ideas.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe how a cultural practice travels from its place of origin to other societies and give reasons for its adoption.
periods.section_context: Yoga's 3,000-year history in India, spread through travellers and scholars, International Day of Yoga on 21 June, yoga poses, harmony with nature and self.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether any student's family practises yoga at home or whether they know of a teacher or elder who introduced them to it — this grounds the global journey in lived experience. If students know yoga in a regional or folk tradition by a different name, celebrate that as evidence of how deeply it has been absorbed.

periods.activity_title: The Chilli's Journey — Globe Tracing and Food Memory
periods.section_ref: Story 3: Chilli—A Spice that Changed our Lives!
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 3: Chilli—A Spice that Changed our Lives! — Students use a coloured string to trace the journey of chillies from South America to India on the globe (p. 168)
materials: Coloured string (one colour per pair, different from migration string used earlier)
periods.visual_aids: Globe; textbook map or image on p. 168 if available

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses a provocation: 'Imagine Indian food without chillies — no red curry, no green chutney, no mirchi bajji. What would you use instead?' Students respond, and teacher introduces the textbook fact: before chillies arrived, black pepper was used to add heat. Students are surprised — teacher asks them to hold that surprise and think about when and how chillies arrived.

Students open Textbook p. 168 and read the chilli story. In pairs, they then use a coloured string on the globe to trace the journey: starting from South America (students locate it on the globe), crossing the Atlantic, arriving in India via the Portuguese trade route. Each pair records in their notebooks: start continent, end continent, approximate direction of travel, and who brought the chilli (Portuguese travellers, 400–500 years ago).

Students explore the second inquiry from Textbook p. 168: 'Potatoes, tomatoes, peanuts, cashews — they all travelled to India. Find out and write the story of any one of them.' Students choose one item and write a short paragraph about its origin and how it reached India. Teacher circulates, prompting: 'When did it arrive? Who brought it? What did people use before it came?'

Students write the Textbook p. 168 reflection: 'Ask your parents and write down the name of any recipe in which they have used black pepper and not red chillies.' Students note the recipe name and reflect: 'Is this an old recipe or a new one? Why might someone still use black pepper?' Teacher closes: 'When you eat that dish at home, you are tasting a piece of history.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can trace the geographic route of a plant or food item across continents and connect its journey to changes in local food culture.
periods.section_context: Chilli origin in South America, Portuguese traders bringing chilli to India 400–500 years ago, black pepper as earlier spice, potatoes, tomatoes, peanuts, cashews as similarly travelled foods, globe-tracing with coloured string.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students to ask at home about a dish that uses black pepper — the elder's response may carry a story about older food traditions. If students name a regional dish with black pepper (like rasam or pepper chicken), accept it as valid evidence of how older spicing traditions persist alongside newer ones.

periods.activity_title: The Sweet Story of Sugar — Discussion on Travelling Foods
periods.section_ref: Story 4: The Sweet Story of Sugar!
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 4: The Sweet Story of Sugar! — Students discuss which Indian food they would choose to share with the world and what new food items might travel in the future (p. 169)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the sugar story from Textbook p. 169 aloud — how India originated the process of making jaggery and refining sugar, how this spread globally through trade, and how rice, mangoes, and bananas from India also spread outward while paper came to India from China. Students listen and then identify: 'What came from India? What came to India from elsewhere?' Teacher records responses in two columns on the board.

Structured discussion on Textbook p. 169: 'If you could choose one Indian food to share with the world, what would it be?' Students discuss in pairs for a few minutes, then share with the class. Teacher asks: 'Why that food? What is special about it? Do you think someone from another country would love it immediately, or would it take time to become popular?' Students connect this to the sugar and chilli stories — some foods take centuries to travel and become familiar.

Second discussion from Textbook p. 169: 'What kind of new food items do you think will travel in the future?' Students brainstorm freely — foods currently popular in their region or country that they think others would enjoy. Teacher draws out the idea that food travel has always been driven by traders, travellers, and curiosity — and that this process continues today through restaurants, the internet, and international students.

Students write in their notebooks: 'Our meals carry flavours and stories from around the globe.' They list three things they ate in the past week and note next to each whether it is likely to be originally from India or from another country. Teacher closes with: 'Every meal you eat is a small version of Earth as a shared home.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect the movement of food items across cultures to the broader process of global exchange and describe how local food habits change over time.
periods.section_context: Jaggery and sugar originating in India, spread of sugar-making globally, rice, mangoes, bananas from India, paper from China, honey as earlier sweetener, future travel of foods.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether anyone has tasted a food recently that was described as 'foreign' — this opens the discussion of how today's novelty may become tomorrow's staple. Encourage students to think of jaggery as something their grandparents might know better than refined sugar, connecting older and newer sweetening traditions.

periods.activity_title: Marigold Across Cultures — Writing About Shared Celebrations
periods.section_ref: Story 5: The Mexican Marigold Moves into India!
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 5: The Mexican Marigold Moves into India! — Students write why both Indian and Mexican cultures use marigolds during festivals and why people in different countries include flowers in celebrations (p. 170–171)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of marigold use in Indian and Mexican festivals (p. 170–171)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens: 'Think of any festival or celebration you have attended. Were flowers involved? What kind? Why do you think flowers are used?' Students share briefly. Teacher then reads the marigold story from Textbook pp. 170–171 — how marigolds originated in Mexico and travelled to India, becoming central to temples, weddings, and festivals including Diwali.

Students write their response to the first task from Textbook p. 170: 'Why do you think both Indian and Mexican cultures use marigolds during their festivals?' Students are encouraged to write at least two reasons, drawing on the story's content — vibrant colour, association with celebration and spirituality — and their own experience of seeing marigolds at festivals. Teacher circulates, prompting: 'What feeling does the orange-yellow colour give you? Could that feeling be the same for someone in Mexico?'

Students write their response to the second task from Textbook p. 171: 'Why do you think people in different countries include flowers in celebrations?' This is a broader, more inferential task. Teacher invites students to think beyond marigolds — roses at weddings, jasmine in temples, chrysanthemums in East Asian traditions — and write two or three reasons why flowers seem to be a universal part of celebration.

Students share one sentence from each of their responses in a round-robin. Class notices: despite different countries and different flowers, similar ideas come up — beauty, fragrance, nature's gift, honouring the occasion. Teacher draws the connection: 'When something from one culture resonates so deeply in another, it is because humans, wherever they live, share certain feelings and needs.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe how a cultural element from one society becomes embedded in another and identify shared human values that explain its adoption.
periods.section_context: Marigold origin in Mexico, adoption into Indian festivals and religious life, Diwali and temple use, orange and yellow colours, flowers in celebrations across cultures.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether their family uses a particular flower for worship or celebration that has a regional name — this surfaces local cultural knowledge about flowers and connects it to the global story. Encourage students to think of their answer to 'why flowers?' as having no single correct response — all thoughtful answers are valid.

periods.activity_title: Indian Cows in Brazil — Inquiry into Animal Travel
periods.section_ref: Story 6: The Cows that Went to Brazil!
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 6: The Cows that Went to Brazil! — Students find out the names of at least five different breeds of cows with help from a teacher or elder (p. 172)
materials: Optional: reference cards or printed list of Indian cattle breeds if available in school
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of Gir, Kankrej, and Ongole cow breeds (p. 172) if available

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the cow story from Textbook p. 172: Portuguese traders took Indian cows — Gir, Kankrej, and Ongole breeds — to Brazil, where they now supply more than three-fourths of the country's milk. These breeds appear on Brazilian stamps and coins. Students are asked: 'Why would traders take cows on a ship across the ocean? What did they know about these breeds that made them worth the journey?'

Students write their response to Textbook p. 171: 'What does this story tell us about animals moving from one place to another?' Two or three sentences minimum. Teacher then transitions to the inquiry activity: the class works together to build a list of at least five breeds of cows, drawing on what students already know (Gir, Kankrej, Ongole from the story) and asking the teacher or any elder who is present for additional breeds.

Students complete the second activity from Textbook p. 172 individually: 'Make a list of a few things in your house or school that may have come from another part of the world — clothing, food, sports equipment, musical instruments, a tree.' Each student lists at least five items and notes next to each where it might originally have come from. Teacher circulates prompting: 'Is your cricket bat from local wood? Where do you think the sport came from?'

Students share their lists in pairs, comparing: did they list the same items or different ones? Which item surprised them most? Whole-class share of two or three surprises. Teacher connects: 'Just as Indian cows transformed Brazilian dairy farming, everyday objects in your home carry journeys you may never have noticed.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify examples of animals or objects that have moved across regions and describe the effect of that movement on a receiving society.
periods.section_context: Gir, Kankrej, and Ongole cow breeds, Portuguese traders taking cows to Brazil, three-fourths of Brazil's milk from Indian breeds, Indian breeds on Brazilian stamps and coins, everyday objects and their global origins.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If there is a student whose family has farming background, invite them to name a cow breed they know — local knowledge about cattle breeds is often rich and regionally specific. The list of everyday items in the second activity will vary widely by region; accept all answers and treat regional variation as evidence of the chapter's core theme.

periods.activity_title: Cultural Diversity Gallery — Observing and Recording Differences
periods.section_ref: Story 2: Yoga—India's Gift to the World!
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 2: Yoga—India's Gift to the World! — Students observe and record how yoga poses are described and depicted in the textbook, connecting the visual descriptions to what yoga is said to do for the body and mind (p. 167)

time_bands.activity: Teacher returns to the yoga section of the textbook (p. 167) and draws students' attention to the images of yoga poses. Students are asked to observe carefully: 'What do you notice about the position of the body in each pose? What parts of the body are used? Does the pose look like something in nature — a tree, a bird, an animal?' Students call out observations; teacher records descriptive words on the board.

Students set up a two-column observation record in their notebooks: 'What the pose looks like' and 'What the textbook says it helps with'. They fill in entries for at least three poses visible in or described in Textbook p. 167. The goal is to observe and record accurately, connecting visual description with stated function — a structured O&R task anchored to the cultural practice.

Whole-class discussion drawing on the observation records: 'The textbook says yoga is about harmony with oneself and with nature. Looking at your observations — do any of the poses remind you of a plant, animal, or natural movement?' Students make connections between pose names or shapes and natural forms. Teacher notes that many yoga pose names in Indian tradition are named after animals and natural elements — this is an example of cultural practice rooted in nature-awareness.

Students write a short observation summary: 'Yoga is a practice that began in India and has spread around the world. From my observation today, I think it became popular because…' — two to three sentences. This consolidates the observation into a reasoned conclusion about cultural spread.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the features of a cultural practice and draw reasoned conclusions about its appeal across different societies.
periods.section_context: Yoga poses and their physical descriptions, harmony with self and nature, yoga's 3,000-year history in India, spread across countries, International Day of Yoga.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether any of the poses have names they recognise from home or a local practice — some students may know pose names in Sanskrit or regional languages, which is evidence of how the practice has been preserved and transmitted. Keep the observation record factual and specific, not impressionistic.

periods.activity_title: Web of Life — Globe Map of Global Journeys
periods.textbook_anchor: Web of Life — Students list things that came to India from other countries and those that went from India to the world, then trace their journeys on a map using two different coloured strings (p. 173)
materials: Globe or large printed world map
Two colours of string or wool per group

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the Web of Life section from Textbook p. 173 by reading the synthesis statement aloud: 'Whether a bird migrates across continents, a seed grows in new soil, or yoga reaches every corner of the globe — we are all connected.' Students are asked: 'From everything we have explored in this chapter, what are some things that came TO India from other places, and what are some things that went FROM India to the world?'

In groups of three or four, students build their two lists (Textbook p. 173) — 'Came to India' and 'Went from India' — drawing from all the stories covered (rosy starlings, yoga, chilli, sugar, marigold, Indian cows). Each group then uses two coloured strings on the globe to trace at least four journeys — two in each direction. One string colour for 'into India' and one for 'out of India'. Students record the journeys in their notebooks alongside the string work.

Groups share their maps with the class — one group traces a journey on the class globe while others observe. Teacher asks: 'Look at the globe with all these strings — what shape do you see? Does it look like a web?' Students observe the density of connections. Teacher connects this to the section's metaphor: Earth is a living web of life where people, animals, plants, and ideas travel, mix, and grow together.

Students write one sentence in their notebooks: 'The Web of Life means…' in their own words. Teacher closes by asking: 'If everything is connected in this web, what happens when one part of it is harmed?' — an open question that leads naturally into the chapter's final section without naming it.

periods.implied_lo: Students can organise evidence of cultural and natural exchange onto a globe and describe the pattern of connections as a global web.
periods.section_context: Web of life synthesis, journeys to India (chilli, marigold, paper), journeys from India (yoga, sugar, Indian cow breeds, rice, mangoes), two-colour string tracing on globe or map.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage groups to debate which direction an item travelled — some students may disagree about whether something is 'Indian' or 'foreign', and that productive disagreement is exactly the chapter's point. Accept all reasoned positions; the quality of the argument matters more than the answer.

periods.activity_title: Interview a Memory — Elder's Story of Change
periods.textbook_anchor: Web of Life — Students interview a grandparent or neighbour about a food item, song, or custom that was not there in their childhood but is common today and find out where it came from (p. 173)
materials: Interview question guide written on board

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens by posing the inquiry question from Textbook p. 173: 'If you interviewed your grandparent or a neighbour about something that did not exist when they were young but is very common now, what would you ask?' Students brainstorm interview questions as a class. Teacher writes the best three or four questions on the board: 'What was not there in your childhood?' 'When did it arrive?' 'Where do you think it came from?' 'How did it change things?'

Since the interview is designed for home, the classroom phase is a preparation and rehearsal activity. Students write their interview questions in their notebooks, choose the food, song, or custom they plan to ask about, and write a hypothesis: 'I think my grandparent will tell me about _____ because _____.' Pairs then practise interviewing each other using the questions, with one student playing the role of a grandparent who has seen a change.

Role-play share: two or three pairs perform their practice interviews briefly for the class. Class identifies: 'Did the interviewer ask a follow-up question? Did the answer tell us where the change came from?' Teacher models one follow-up question: 'You said this arrived when you were young — who brought it to your town? Was it a traveller, a relative, a shop?' This models the C-2.3 skill of connecting change to a source.

Students write in their notebooks: 'The change I plan to ask my grandparent or neighbour about is ___. I think it came from ___. I want to know ___.' This is their inquiry plan. Teacher closes by connecting to the chapter's theme: 'When we listen to elders, we are tracing our own family's small thread in the Web of Life.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can design simple inquiry questions to investigate how cultural practices change over time as communicated by elders.
periods.section_context: Elder interview about a food, song, or custom new since their childhood, change communicated by grandparent or neighbour, Web of Life synthesis of cultural exchange.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Acknowledge that not all students have easy access to grandparents — suggest that a neighbour, a shopkeeper, or an older teacher in the school can serve as the elder for this inquiry. The interview does not need to happen in a formal sitting; a short conversation at home counts fully.

periods.activity_title: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam — Exploring the One-Family Idea
periods.textbook_anchor: One Earth, One Family! — Students write the meaning of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam in their own words and discuss how we can live like one big family even when we are different (p. 176)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image of the MoEFCC logo (p. 176) if available

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' on the board and asks: 'Has anyone heard this before? Does anyone know what it means?' Students share guesses. Teacher then reads the closing section from Textbook p. 176, explaining the concept — the world is one family, extending to all people, animals, trees, rivers, air, and sky. Students are asked: 'Which part of this idea surprised you most? What is included in this family that you did not expect?'

Students write two responses from Textbook p. 176: first, what does 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' teach us? Second, write its meaning in their own words. Teacher emphasises that the second task is NOT a translation — it is their own way of expressing the idea, in whatever language feels natural to them. Students who want to write in a home language first and then translate are encouraged to do so.

Discussion on Textbook p. 176: 'How can we live like one big family, even when we are different?' Students work in groups of four, generating at least three concrete behaviours — not abstract values, but things a person actually does: sharing food, learning a word in another language, helping someone who is lost, not littering in a space others share. Groups report back; teacher records behaviours on the board.

Teacher draws attention to the MoEFCC logo (Textbook p. 176) as a symbol of balance between nature and human life. Students discuss: 'What does it mean to say that caring for the Earth is the same as caring for your family?' Class reaches a shared statement together, which the teacher writes on the board and students copy as a closing reflection.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain a philosophical concept about social and environmental responsibility in their own words and give concrete examples of how it can be practised.
periods.section_context: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam — world as one family, Earth as the only planet with life, MoEFCC logo, caring for Earth as caring for each other, all living beings as family members.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether they know any other saying in their home language that expresses a similar idea — many Indian languages have folk sayings about the earth as mother or about shared belonging. These folk expressions are equally valid articulations of the concept and connect it to the student's lived cultural context.

periods.activity_title: Caring for Our Shared Home — Writing Actions and Commitments
periods.textbook_anchor: One Earth, One Family! — Students write one way they can care for the Earth and identify an item that can travel from India to other parts of the world (p. 176)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a gentle provocation: 'The textbook says Earth has supported living beings for thousands of years and that it needs care. What does it mean for a planet to need care? What happens when care is not given?' Students discuss in pairs and share. Teacher connects: 'Caring for the Earth is not something that happens far away — it happens in small choices made every day, right here.'

Students write their response to the first 'Let us reflect' task from Textbook p. 176: 'Write one way you can care for the Earth.' The instruction is to write at least one specific, concrete action — not 'be good to nature' but 'I will carry a cloth bag when I go to the market' or 'I will not waste water when I brush my teeth.' Teacher circulates, pushing for specificity: 'What will you do? When? Where?' Students may write more than one action if inspired.

Students write their response to the third 'Let us reflect' task from Textbook p. 176: 'Identify an item that can travel from India to other parts of the world and write about it.' Students pick any item — a food, a craft, a musical instrument, a sport — and write about why it might appeal to people in other countries, drawing on what they have learned through the chapter's stories.

Class shares their Earth-care actions in a brief round. Teacher notices patterns — water, waste, plants, animals — and draws out: 'Every action you named protects one part of the web of life. When you water a plant, you are not just being kind to a plant — you are maintaining one thread in the web.' Students write a final one-sentence commitment in their notebooks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can articulate specific actions that express a sense of responsibility towards the Earth and connect those actions to a broader ethical framework.
periods.section_context: Writing one way to care for the Earth, identifying an Indian item that can travel to the world, Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam as ethical framework, Earth as the only known planet with life.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Affirm that any genuinely practised small action is as valuable as a grand gesture — this avoids the chapter's values becoming merely rhetorical. Ask: 'Is there something your family already does that cares for the Earth, perhaps something a grandparent taught?' This surfaces traditional conservation practices as equally valid Earth-care.

periods.activity_title: A Travelled Idea — Writing the Story of a Journey
periods.textbook_anchor: One Earth, One Family! — Students pick one idea and write a short story about how it might have travelled from one place to another long ago and how it helped people change their lives (p. 176)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the 'Let us reflect' prompt from Textbook p. 176 aloud: 'Pick one of the ideas. Write a short story about how this idea might have travelled from one place to another long ago. Think about how it helped people change their lives or the way they think.' Students are given a brief brainstorm time: 'Which idea from the chapter interests you most? Which journey made you most curious?' Students name their choices aloud — teacher notes the variety.

Students write their short story independently. The story must include: an idea, practice, plant, animal, or food that travelled; where it started; how it travelled (a person, a trade ship, a wind, a bird?); where it arrived; and one way it changed the receiving community's lives or thinking. Teacher circulates with prompts for students who are stuck: 'Imagine you are the person who first tasted chilli in India, or the first person in another country to learn a yoga pose — what did you feel? What did you do next?'

Students share their stories in groups of three by reading them aloud. Group members identify: 'Did the story include a journey? Did it show how the receiving people were changed?' Each group chooses one story to share with the whole class. Two or three stories are read aloud; class offers one appreciative observation for each.

Teacher closes by connecting all the stories heard: 'Every story you just told is true, in its own way — things do travel like this, and they do change people. That is what this chapter has been about: Earth is a home where ideas, living things, and stories are always in motion.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can construct a narrative that traces the journey of an idea or cultural element across societies and articulates its transformative effect.
periods.section_context: Writing a short story about a travelled idea from the chapter, journey of idea or practice or plant or animal, change in the receiving community, 'Let us reflect' narrative task.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage students to draw on any story from the chapter — there is no required topic. Students who find narrative writing difficult may structure their story as a simple sequence: 'First… Then… Finally…' Students who are more confident writers may experiment with dialogue or a first-person voice.

periods.activity_title: Earth — Our Shared Home: Chapter Synthesis
periods.textbook_anchor: Web of Life — Students synthesise the chapter's stories by reflecting on the single connecting truth: all living things, ideas, and people are part of one web of life on a shared Earth (p. 173)
periods.visual_aids: Globe if available; textbook pp. 162–176 for reference

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a large circle on the board labelled 'Earth — Our Shared Home' and says: 'This chapter told us many stories — about birds, a spice, a sweetener, a flower, cows, a practice, and a philosophy. What is the single idea that connects all of them?' Students call out responses. Teacher records keywords around the circle: migration, travel, trade, culture, nature, connection, care, family.

Structured whole-class discussion: Teacher poses three synthesis questions one at a time, giving students time to think and respond. First: 'What do the rosy starlings, the chilli, the marigold, and the Indian cow breeds have in common?' Second: 'What do yoga, sugar, and Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam have in common?' Third: 'If Earth has no borders for nature, what does that mean for how humans should treat each other and the planet?' Students respond to each; teacher draws connecting lines on the board between the keywords.

Students write a synthesis paragraph in their notebooks — three to five sentences answering the question: 'What does it mean to say Earth is our shared home?' The paragraph must draw on at least three specific examples from the chapter (they may choose any). Teacher circulates, prompting: 'Can you name something specific — a bird, a food, a practice — to support your idea? Can you connect one natural story to one human-cultural story?'

Students share their synthesis paragraphs in pairs — each reads, the partner identifies the three examples used and says whether the central idea came through clearly. Two or three paragraphs are shared with the whole class. Teacher closes with the chapter's final statement from Textbook p. 173: 'Caring for each other and the planet makes us part of that connection.' Students write this as the last line of their notebook page for this chapter.

periods.implied_lo: Students can synthesise evidence from multiple chapter examples to articulate a single unifying argument about global interconnection and shared responsibility.
periods.section_context: Synthesis of all chapter stories: rosy starlings, yoga, chilli, sugar, marigold, Indian cow breeds, Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, web of life, Earth as shared home, global connections between natural and human-cultural strands.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: This synthesis works with what any class has actually encountered in this chapter — whether they covered all the stories or only some, the connecting idea holds. Accept synthesis paragraphs that use any combination of examples from the chapter; breadth of examples is less important than the clarity of the connecting argument.

assessment_items.question_text: A student uses a globe and finds that the Pacific Ocean, the Atlantic Ocean, and the Indian Ocean are all joined to each other without any land breaking them apart. What does this show about Earth's oceans?

options.label: A
options.text: Each ocean is a separate body of water surrounded by land on all sides.

options.label: B
options.text: Earth's oceans form one connected body of water with no natural barrier between them.

options.label: C
options.text: Oceans are connected only where rivers flow into them.

options.label: D
options.text: The oceans are connected only near the North Pole.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. This item tests globe-reading and the ability to articulate a geographic observation about natural connectivity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can locate geographic features on a globe and articulate why natural features do not align with human-made boundaries.

competency.competency_text: Reads simple maps of city, state, and country to identify natural and humanmade features (well, lake, post office, school, hospital) with reference to symbols and directions

what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates the student believes oceans are isolated like landlocked lakes — a misconception about what a globe shows when tracing ocean boundaries.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses river systems with ocean connectivity — shows the student has not observed ocean shapes on the globe but has recalled an unrelated water-connection idea.
what_each_option_reveals.D: A partial memory of polar geography, possibly confusing Arctic sea ice with actual ocean connection — shows recall of a geographic detail applied incorrectly.

assessment_items.question_text: Rosy starlings fly thousands of kilometres from Russia and Mongolia to India every winter. Give two reasons why this migration benefits both the birds and Indian farmers.
expected_elements: Birds benefit: they find warm weather in India that allows them to survive the winter.
Farmers benefit: the birds feed on locusts and grasshoppers, which are crop pests, reducing crop damage.
assessment_items.annotation: A complete response names one benefit for each party. Accept equivalent phrasing. This item tests ability to read a migration route as meaningful — not just movement but mutual benefit — as developed through the string-tracing and discussion activity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use a globe to trace a migration route and record directional observations about movement across geographic boundaries.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: Birds find warm weather (or food availability) in India that sustains them through winter.
Farmers benefit because rosy starlings eat locusts and grasshoppers, which damage crops.

assessment_items.question_text: A student made a poster of winter birds in their area. For one bird on the poster, they wrote: 'Name — Crane. Comes from — Siberia, Russia. Stays in — wetlands and fields.' What inquiry steps did the student follow to produce this entry?
expected_elements: The student identified a specific bird by name rather than a general description.
The student found out where the bird comes from — its country or region of origin.
The student noted the habitat or location where the bird is found locally.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any bird name and origin the student mentions — regionally varied answers are acceptable and correct. The focus is on identifying the inquiry steps (name, origin, habitat) not on the specific bird chosen.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple guided inquiry to identify local examples of a natural phenomenon and record their findings in a visual format.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Identified the bird by a specific name (not just 'a bird').
Found out the bird's place of origin (country or region it comes from).
Noted where the bird is found locally or what it eats — at least one observed detail beyond the name.

assessment_items.task: Imagine you are a rosy starling flying from Mongolia to India. Write a short postcard to a friend back home. In your postcard, mention: (a) one thing you see or notice during the journey, and (b) one thing in nature that helps you travel.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My postcard:
Dear friend,
I am writing to you from ___. On my way here I noticed ___. What helped me travel was ___.
Your friend,
[Your bird name]
format_of_output: May include a small sketch on the reverse side
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any factual natural detail (mountains, rivers, changing landscapes, warm air, wind currents, ocean currents) and any natural travel aid. The postcard need not be long — two or three sentences that include both required elements earn full credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present observations about a natural process through a creative written mode, including factual details within an imaginative format.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can embed accurate natural-science content (migration aids, observed landscape) within a creative first-person format — testing both factual recall and expressive skill.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts the two required elements directly. A student who fills in both blanks with specific content meets the standard. Vague fill-ins ('something nice', 'the weather') do not meet the standard.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: names a specific landscape feature or natural phenomenon seen during migration AND names a specific travel aid (warm air, wind, ocean current). Weak: mentions only feelings or generic descriptions with no factual content from the chapter.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find English difficult may write in a home language first; a brief translation or the teacher's verbal report of content suffices. A student may also draw the postcard and describe it orally to the teacher.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The postcard format matches the chapter task exactly and constrains length naturally, making the assessment executable within a single session without craft materials.

assessment_items.question_text: Yoga began in India about 3,000 years ago. Today, people in almost every country practise it, and the United Nations declared 21 June as the International Day of Yoga. Which best explains how yoga spread to so many countries?

options.label: A
options.text: The United Nations made it compulsory for all countries to practise yoga.

options.label: B
options.text: Travellers, scholars, and teachers from India carried the practice to other parts of the world over many centuries.

options.label: C
options.text: Yoga was invented separately in many countries at the same time.

options.label: D
options.text: Yoga spread because it is the only exercise that keeps people healthy.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. This item tests whether students can identify the mechanism of cultural spread (human carriers over time) rather than an institutional or coincidental explanation.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Story 2: Yoga—India's Gift to the World!
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe how a cultural practice travels from its place of origin to other societies and give reasons for its adoption.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses a recognition of yoga (UN declaration) with a mandate — shows the student misread the role of international organisations as enforcers rather than acknowledgers.
what_each_option_reveals.C: A parallel-invention idea that ignores the textbook's explanation — shows the student did not engage with the story of how yoga travelled through people.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Focuses on a quality of yoga (health benefit) rather than the mechanism of its spread — shows the student recalls that yoga is beneficial but has not connected this to how cultural practices travel.

assessment_items.question_text: Chillies came to India from South America about 400–500 years ago, brought by Portuguese travellers. Before chillies arrived, Indians used a different ingredient to make food spicy. (a) Name that ingredient. (b) Explain one way the arrival of chillies changed Indian food culture.
expected_elements: (a) Black pepper was used to add spice to food before chillies arrived.
(b) Any one valid change: chilli became central to Indian cuisine / replaced or reduced the use of black pepper in many dishes / new dishes and flavour profiles developed using chilli.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept 'pepper', 'black pepper', or 'kali mirch' for part (a). For part (b), accept any reasonable food-culture change connected to the chapter's content. Regionally varied answers are acceptable — students may name a local dish that now uses chilli where older versions used pepper.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Story 3: Chilli—A Spice that Changed our Lives!
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace the geographic route of a plant or food item across continents and connect its journey to changes in local food culture.

competency.competency_text: Connects changes in the environment and the lives of their family and community, as communicated by elders and through local stories (changes in occupation, food habits, resources, celebrations, communication)

expected_elements: Names black pepper (or equivalent) as the spice used before chillies.

Describes at least one concrete change in food culture following the arrival of chillies — such as chilli becoming central to Indian cooking, replacing black pepper in many dishes, or enabling new recipes.

assessment_items.question_text: The textbook says that India gave sugar to the world, while China gave paper to India. Meals today carry 'flavours and stories from around the globe.' Using two or more examples from the chapter, explain what this means and why it matters.
look_for: Uses at least two specific examples of food or material exchange from the chapter (e.g. sugar from India, paper from China, chilli from South America, rice and mangoes from India).
Explains that the exchange is two-directional — things travel both to and from India.
Connects the exchange to how daily life (food, writing, cooking) was changed by these journeys.
Offers a reason why this pattern of exchange matters — such as showing that no culture is self-sufficient, or that shared resources create shared histories.
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response uses named examples, shows bidirectionality, and makes a reasoned claim about significance. A weak response lists examples without connecting them to the main idea. Accept any valid examples from the chapter.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Story 4: The Sweet Story of Sugar!
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect the movement of food items across cultures to the broader process of global exchange and describe how local food habits change over time.

competency.competency_text: Connects changes in the environment and the lives of their family and community, as communicated by elders and through local stories (changes in occupation, food habits, resources, celebrations, communication)

look_for: At least two named examples of exchange drawn from the chapter.
Recognition that exchange flows in both directions — into and out of India.
A connection between a specific exchange and a change in daily life (food, writing materials, cooking methods).
A reasoned statement about why this matters — beyond simple description, a claim about human interdependence or shared history.

assessment_items.question_text: Marigolds originally came from Mexico. Today in India, they are used in temples, weddings, and festivals like Diwali. Give two reasons why you think marigolds became so deeply embedded in Indian culture even though they came from another country.
expected_elements: Any one reason related to the flower's natural qualities: its vibrant orange and yellow colour resonated with Indian associations with warmth, celebration, and spirituality.
Any one reason related to shared human values: both Indian and Mexican cultures use flowers in festivals and celebrations — the flower met a cultural need that already existed.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two reasoned responses grounded in the chapter content. Regionally varied answers are acceptable — students who reference a local festival or cultural use of marigolds in their region are demonstrating the same understanding.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Story 5: The Mexican Marigold Moves into India!
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe how a cultural element from one society becomes embedded in another and identify shared human values that explain its adoption.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

expected_elements: A reason related to the flower's appearance or quality — vibrant colour, long-lasting, fragrant, or abundant — that suited Indian festival aesthetics.
A reason related to cultural compatibility — flowers were already valued in Indian religious and celebratory life, so the marigold met an existing need.

assessment_items.question_text: Portuguese traders took Indian cows — including the Gir, Kankrej, and Ongole breeds — to Brazil. Today, these breeds provide more than three-fourths of Brazil's milk, and they appear on Brazilian stamps and coins. What does this tell us about the effect of animals moving from one region to another?
expected_elements: Animals can thrive in new environments when conditions suit them.
The movement of Indian cow breeds transformed Brazil's dairy farming — they became so important that they are celebrated in Brazilian national symbols (stamps and coins).
Animals, like plants and ideas, can cross continents and become central to the economy and culture of a new society.
assessment_items.annotation: A complete response draws on at least two of the expected elements. The stamps and coins detail is a useful marker of a thorough response — it shows the student engaged with the evidence of lasting impact.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Story 6: The Cows that Went to Brazil!
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify examples of animals or objects that have moved across regions and describe the effect of that movement on a receiving society.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: States that Indian cow breeds thrived in Brazil's environment.
Notes a concrete impact: supplying more than three-fourths of Brazil's milk, or appearing on stamps and coins as a sign of cultural significance.
Makes a broader observation: animals, like plants and ideas, can cross continents and become important to the receiving society.

assessment_items.question_text: A student observed the images of yoga poses in the textbook and recorded: 'The Tree Pose — standing on one leg, arms raised, body balanced. The textbook says it helps with concentration and balance.' Which skill did the student use to produce this record?

options.label: A
options.text: The student made up information about yoga from their own imagination.

options.label: B
options.text: The student observed the pose carefully and recorded what it looks like and what the textbook says it does.

options.label: C
options.text: The student interviewed a yoga teacher to find out about the pose.

options.label: D
options.text: The student tested the pose themselves and recorded how it felt.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. This item tests whether students can identify the observe-and-record method as distinct from invention, interview, or hands-on testing.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Story 2: Yoga—India's Gift to the World!
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the features of a cultural practice and draw reasoned conclusions about its appeal across different societies.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student thinks recording is a creative act rather than an observational one — a misconception about the nature of observation records.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses the observe-and-record method with an interview inquiry — the student may not distinguish between reading a source (textbook) and interviewing a person.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses observation of a visual source with physical experimentation — shows the student has not identified that the record came from watching an image, not from doing the pose.

assessment_items.question_text: A student used a globe and two coloured strings to show: one string for things that came TO India from other countries, and one string for things that went FROM India to the world. They listed: chilli (South America → India), yoga (India → world), sugar (India → world), marigold (Mexico → India), paper (China → India). (a) Which string colour represents things that came to India? Give two examples from the list. (b) What does the pattern of all these strings together show about Earth?
expected_elements: (a) The string for 'came to India' represents: chilli (from South America), marigold (from Mexico), and paper (from China) — any two of these three.
(b) The pattern shows that Earth is a web of connections — things, ideas, and living beings travel in many directions between many places, making Earth a shared home.
assessment_items.annotation: Part (a) requires correct identification of direction. Part (b) should describe the overall pattern — accept any phrasing that conveys interconnection, web, or shared exchange rather than one-directional flow.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can organise evidence of cultural and natural exchange onto a globe and describe the pattern of connections as a global web.

competency.competency_text: Reads simple maps of city, state, and country to identify natural and humanmade features (well, lake, post office, school, hospital) with reference to symbols and directions

expected_elements: Correctly identifies the 'to India' string and names two examples from the list: chilli, marigold, or paper.
Describes the combined pattern as showing global interconnection — that exchange flows in multiple directions between many countries, not just one way.

assessment_items.question_text: A student planned to interview their grandmother about a food that was not common when the grandmother was young but is eaten regularly today. Write two interview questions the student should ask to find out (a) what the food is and (b) how it arrived or became popular in their community.
expected_elements: A question that asks the grandmother to name a food that was not available or common in her childhood (e.g. 'What food do we eat today that you did not have when you were young?').

A question that probes how the food arrived or became popular (e.g. 'When did this food first come to our area?' or 'How did people in our family or community start eating it?' or 'Where did it come from originally?').
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any open-ended question that achieves the two purposes. Closed yes/no questions do not meet the standard. Regionally varied answers are acceptable — the food named or the community described may vary widely by region.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design simple inquiry questions to investigate how cultural practices change over time as communicated by elders.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: One open question that asks the elder to identify a food (or song or custom) new since their childhood.
One open question that probes the source or route of arrival of that food — when it came, where it came from, or how the community came to adopt it.

assessment_items.question_text: 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' is an ancient Indian idea that says the world is one family. The textbook says this family includes not just people but also animals, trees, rivers, air, and sky. Using this idea, explain: (a) what it means to treat the Earth as family, and (b) one specific thing a person can do to act on this idea in daily life.
look_for: Explains that treating Earth as family means extending care and responsibility beyond one's immediate human circle to include living and non-living parts of the natural world.
Connects the idea that harming one part of the family (e.g. a river, a tree, air) harms the whole — including people.
Gives a specific, concrete daily action — not a vague value statement — that enacts this sense of shared family responsibility.
Shows awareness that the idea is ancient and Indian in origin, placing it in its cultural-philosophical context.
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response explains the concept, applies it to non-human nature, and gives a specific personal action. A weak response restates the phrase without explaining it or gives a generic 'be kind to nature' without specificity. Accept any valid personal action.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain a philosophical concept about social and environmental responsibility in their own words and give concrete examples of how it can be practised.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

look_for: Explains Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam in the student's own words — not a translation but an interpretation.
Extends the family idea beyond people to include animals, plants, rivers, air — acknowledging the full scope of the concept.
Connects care for non-human nature to care for humans — showing the logic that harming one part harms all.
Names a specific, observable daily action (not a vague aspiration) that demonstrates the one-family ethic.

assessment_items.task: Think about what you have learned about how things travel across the world — birds, foods, practices, and ideas. Write one specific thing you will do to care for the Earth. Then explain why that action matters, using an example from the chapter.
assessment_items.scaffold:
The action I will take: ___
Why this matters: ___
An example from the chapter that connects to my action: ___
format_of_output: Three clearly addressed parts: action, reason, chapter connection
assessment_items.annotation: A complete response names a specific action, gives a reason rooted in the chapter's argument, and connects it to at least one example (a bird, a plant, a practice, a philosophy). Accept any valid action and any chapter example. Regionally varied actions are acceptable and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can articulate specific actions that express a sense of responsibility towards the Earth and connect those actions to a broader ethical framework.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can move from ethical understanding to personal commitment — naming a specific, doable action and grounding it in the chapter's evidence rather than generic good intentions.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The three-part scaffold is the assessment structure: action (specific, not vague), reason (drawn from chapter logic), and chapter connection (a named example). All three must be present for a complete response.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: specific action (e.g. 'I will not waste water when washing'), a reason that connects to the web of life or Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, and a named chapter example. Weak: vague action ('be nice to nature'), no reason, or no chapter connection.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may describe an action their family already practises — a traditional conservation behaviour counts fully. Students who find writing difficult may draw their action and explain it orally to the teacher.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The three-part scaffold matches the chapter's move from idea to action, ensuring the response tests both understanding and personal application within a manageable length.

assessment_items.task: Choose one thing from the chapter that travelled from one place to another — it can be a bird, a food, a plant, an animal, or a practice. Write a short story (4–6 sentences) about its journey. Your story must include: where it started, how it travelled, where it arrived, and one way it changed the lives of people in the new place.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My story:
Once, ___ lived in ___.
One day / Long ago, it travelled to ___ because ___.
When it arrived, people found that ___.
Because of this, ___.
format_of_output: Must address: origin, method of travel, destination, impact on receiving community
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any element from the chapter as the subject of the story. The four required elements (origin, travel, destination, impact) are the assessment criteria — not the specific subject chosen. A story about any chapter element that addresses all four earns full credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a narrative that traces the journey of an idea or cultural element across societies and articulates its transformative effect.

competency.competency_text: Connects changes in the environment and the lives of their family and community, as communicated by elders and through local stories (changes in occupation, food habits, resources, celebrations, communication)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can take the chapter's core concept — things travel and transform the places they reach — and express it in a narrative structure that includes all four required elements.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Each blank in the scaffold maps to one required element. A story that skips a blank is incomplete. The teacher should check: Is there an origin? A method of travel? A destination? A stated impact?
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: four elements clearly present, specific content from the chapter, and an impact that describes a real change (not just 'people liked it'). Weak: missing one or more elements, or impact is vague ('it was good for them').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may choose any chapter subject — there is no required element. Students who prefer drawing may sketch the journey as a four-panel comic with captions, which counts as equivalent. Students may write in a home language if needed.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Short narrative with four structural elements
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The narrative format matches the chapter's own storytelling mode and tests the student's ability to sequence a journey — origin, movement, arrival, impact — which is the chapter's core argument made concrete.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter tells us about rosy starlings from Russia, chillies from South America, yoga from India, marigolds from Mexico, and Indian cow breeds in Brazil. All of these are different — birds, spices, practices, flowers, and animals. Yet the chapter says they all point to one truth. What is that truth? Use at least three examples from the chapter to explain your answer.
look_for: States the unifying truth clearly: Earth is a shared home where people, animals, plants, and ideas are all connected — no single culture or country exists in isolation.
Uses at least three specific examples from the chapter — drawn from different categories (natural and human-cultural) — to support the claim.
Shows that the examples are not just a list but are linked to the central argument about interconnection.
Demonstrates awareness of both strands: that natural phenomena (bird migration, plant travel) and human-cultural exchange (yoga, sugar, trade) are part of the same web.
Optionally references Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam or the Web of Life as the chapter's philosophical conclusion.
assessment_items.annotation: This is the synthesis assessment item. A strong response names the central truth, uses examples from both the natural and human-cultural strands, and makes a reasoned argument rather than a list. Accept any three chapter examples; breadth of selection is less important than quality of reasoning.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can synthesise evidence from multiple chapter examples to articulate a single unifying argument about global interconnection and shared responsibility.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

look_for: A clear statement of the unifying truth — Earth is a shared home; all living things, ideas, and people are connected.
At least three specific chapter examples, ideally drawn from both natural (birds, plants, animals) and human-cultural (yoga, sugar, marigold, Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam) strands.
Examples used as evidence for the argument, not merely listed.
A conclusion that connects the examples back to the central claim about shared responsibility or global interdependence.
